title: Deep Dive: Java 21 Virtual Threads (Project Loom) vs Reactive Streams in Microservices
summary: Comprehensive architectural comparison of Thread-per-Request concurrency with Virtual Threads against Reactive Programming (Project Reactor/RxJava) across performance, syntax clarity, and observability.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.problem-statement: Prior to Java 21, handling tens of thousands of concurrent connections with blocking I/O required rewriting code to Reactive Streams (Spring WebFlux, RxJava). However, reactive pipelines introduce steep cognitive complexity, fragmented stack traces, and fragile ThreadLocal contexts.
sections.initial-approach: Standard Platform Threads (1 Java Thread = 1 OS Thread) hit hard limits around 2,000 - 3,000 threads due to 1MB stack memory allocations and costly OS context switching overhead.
sections.optimization-thinking:
Java 21 Virtual Threads (Project Loom) introduces lightweight user-mode threads scheduled by the JVM:

  • Millions of Virtual Threads run on a small pool of Carrier OS threads.
  • Upon encountering blocking I/O (JDBC queries, outbound REST calls), the JVM automatically unmounts the virtual thread without blocking the underlying carrier thread.
  • Enables writing straightforward, sequential code with crystal-clear stack traces.
sections.code-implementation:
Enabling Virtual Threads in Spring Boot 3.2+ is as simple as configuring spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true or utilizing ExecutorService:

try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
  IntStream.range(0, 100_000).forEach(i -> executor.submit(() -> {
    fetchRemoteApi(i);
  }));
}
sections.complexity-applications: Delivers 90-95% of Reactive Streams throughput with 50% lower maintenance overhead. Ideal for I/O-bound microservices, enterprise CRUD APIs, and payment orchestrators.

title: Tech Lead Insights: Balancing Technical Debt and Feature Delivery Velocity
summary: A pragmatic engineering governance framework to maintain codebase health, prevent operational outages, and sustain business feature delivery commitments.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.introduction: One of the primary challenges for a Technical Team Lead is balancing commercial pressure for rapid feature delivery against the vital need to address technical debt and preserve system stability.
sections.multi-dimensional-evaluation:
Categorizing technical debt into 3 distinct quadrants:

  • Deliberate Debt: Consciously taking shortcuts to validate market hypotheses with a committed refactoring plan within 1 sprint.
  • Architectural Decay: Legacy systems outgrown by current scale requirements.
  • Accidental Debt: Incurred via rushed code reviews, missing automated tests, or junior knowledge gaps.
sections.case-study-experience: Adopted The 20% Sprint Budget Rule: Allocating a fixed 20% of story points in every sprint toward architectural refactoring, security upgrades, and test automation. Outcome: Production defect rates dropped by 60% across 3 quarters.
sections.actionable-recommendations: Quantify technical debt in financial and business terms (e.g. estimated outage costs, engineer hours lost per sprint) when aligning priorities with Product Managers and Executives.
sections.open-questions-discussion: How does your organization prioritize technical debt alongside feature roadmaps? What strategies have worked best for your team?

title: Designing Absolute Idempotent Payment & Webhook Processing in Distributed Systems
summary: Protecting financial transactions against duplicate webhook deliveries using Distributed Locks, Idempotency Keys, and Transactional Outbox patterns.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.context-problem: Payment gateways (Stripe, VNPay, MoMo) frequently retry webhooks upon transient network timeouts. Without robust idempotency handling, user wallets risk double-crediting or duplicate order fulfillment.
sections.system-requirements:
• Financial Correctness: Zero tolerance for double-spending or duplicate order processing.
  • Performance: Sub-300ms webhook acknowledgment response times to external providers.
sections.architecture-design:
Multi-layered defensive architecture:

  • Tier 1 (Idempotency Key Store): PostgreSQL table enforcing unique constraints on PRIMARY KEY (provider_name, idempotency_key).
  • Tier 2 (Distributed Redis Lock): Temporary mutex locking with SET lock_key token NX PX 5000 during active transaction execution.
  • Tier 3 (Strict State Machine): Enforcing unidirectional state transitions (e.g. PENDING -> PAID, rejecting duplicate PAID transitions).
sections.trade-offs-analysis:
Pessimistic vs Optimistic concurrency control:

  • Optimistic locking with version counters handles general order updates efficiently.
  • Pessimistic Redis distributed locks are applied to critical financial balance debits to guarantee race-free mutations.
sections.lessons-best-practices: Persist raw webhook payloads to audit tables prior to processing, and return immediate HTTP 200 OK responses if a duplicate key has already been settled successfully.

title: Implementing High-Performance Slowly Changing Dimensions (SCD Type 2) in Big Data ETL Pipelines
summary: Tracking historical customer and product attribute mutations over time with dbt, PostgreSQL, and high-performance temporal range indexes.
author: Huỳnh Nhật Tân

sections.business-data-requirements: When customers update shipping addresses or loyalty tiers (VIP to Diamond), historical revenue reports must reflect the customer's tier at the time of purchase rather than overwriting past transactions.
sections.data-modeling:
SCD Type 2 dimensional modeling schema:

  • surrogate_key: Unique synthetic primary key for each record revision.
  • valid_from & valid_to: Temporal validity boundaries (e.g., 9999-12-31 for active records).
  • is_current: Boolean flag marking active current revisions.
sections.pipeline-construction:
Automated snapshotting with dbt (data build tool):

  • Apply check or timestamp strategies to automatically capture delta mutations.
  • Execute atomic MERGE statements to expire old revisions (UPDATE valid_to = now()) and insert new versions.
sections.testing-optimization: Created GiST (customer_id, daterange(valid_from, valid_to)) exclusion constraints to mathematically prevent overlapping validity windows across versions of the same entity.
sections.summary-recommendations: SCD Type 2 is vital for historical reporting integrity. Recommendation: Apply SCD Type 2 selectively to high-value dimensions (Customers, Products) rather than high-frequency telemetry tables.
